chapters.name: Chapter 1: What leaders need to know about AI

lessons.title: Lesson 1: AI in plain words
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain AI, machine learning and generative AI in one sentence each.
This lesson builds toward: When a team member asks what AI is, you will explain AI, machine learning and generative AI in plain words, in one sentence each that a new team member would understand.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is software that does tasks that usually need human judgment, such as recognizing speech, spotting patterns or writing text. Machine learning is the most common way to build it: instead of writing every rule, people show the software many examples and it learns patterns.
Generative AI is machine learning that creates new content: text, images, audio, code. Tools such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini and Claude are built on large language models (LLMs) trained on huge amounts of writing. They predict likely words, which is why they write fluently and also why they can be confidently wrong.
As a leader you do not need the math. You need three plain sentences you can say to your team, and the judgment to know when the tool is helping and when it is guessing.
Words to know:
- Artificial intelligence (AI): software that does tasks that usually need human judgment.
- Machine learning: building software by showing it examples so it learns patterns.
- Generative AI: AI that creates new text, images, audio or code.
- LLM: large language model: the AI behind chat assistants.
Try it now: Write your own one-sentence explanation of AI, machine learning and generative AI, in words your newest team member would understand. Read them out loud.
You can now explain AI, machine learning and generative AI in plain words.

options: Software that learns patterns from examples
A robot that learns to walk
A person teaching a computer by hand, rule by rule
Software that never makes mistakes
check.why: Machine learning finds patterns in examples instead of following hand-written rules.

check.q: A new team member asks what generative AI is. Which answer would you give?
options: It is a search engine with a new name
It is software that only does maths
It is AI that creates new text, images or code from what you ask
It is a program that knows every fact
check.why: Generative AI creates new content; it does not know every fact.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: From assistant to agent: what agentic AI changes
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain the difference between an AI assistant and an AI agent, and why it matters for leaders.
This lesson builds toward: Given a routine team task, you will describe what an AI assistant and an AI agent would each do and which steps a person should approve, naming who stays accountable.
An AI assistant answers when asked: you prompt, it drafts, you decide. An AI agent is given a goal and acts: it plans steps, uses tools such as email, calendars, spreadsheets or websites, checks results and continues until it is done or stopped.
Agentic AI moves AI from advice to action. An assistant drafts a reply to a customer; an agent could read the inbox, draft replies, send them and update the customer record. That saves more time, and it can make mistakes at speed, in your organization's name.
For leaders, the key questions change. Not only "is the answer good?" but "what is it allowed to do, who approves its actions, and who is accountable when it gets something wrong?" A person is always accountable.
Words to know:
- Agentic AI: AI that works toward a goal by planning steps and taking actions with tools.
- Accountable: the person who answers for the result, good or bad.
Try it now: Pick one routine task on your team. Describe what an AI assistant would do for it, and what an AI agent might do. Write which steps you would want a person to approve.
You can now explain how agentic AI differs from an assistant and what leaders must decide.

check.q: What can an AI agent do that a basic assistant does not?
options: Answer a question when asked
Plan steps and take actions with tools toward a goal
Draft a short email
Fix its own mistakes without anyone knowing
check.why: Agents plan and act with tools, which is why leaders must decide what they may do.

check.q: An agent could send refund emails to customers on its own. What would you decide first?
options: Let it send everything to save time
Ban all AI on the team
Let the agent decide which refunds need a person
Which steps a person must approve and who is accountable
check.why: With agents, the leader's question is what it may do, who approves and who is accountable.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: What AI does well and where it fails
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Sort tasks into good, careful and poor uses of AI.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of your team's tasks, you will sort each task into good, careful or poor uses of AI, with a short reason for each.
AI does well at first drafts (emails, job posts, agendas), summarizing long documents, brainstorming options, rewriting for a different audience, and explaining unfamiliar topics. These save time because a person still reviews the result.
Use care with anything factual, legal, financial, medical or about people: AI can make up facts, sources and numbers (often called hallucination), can reflect bias in its training data, and does not know your organization's policies unless you tell it.
Poor uses: final decisions about people (hiring, firing, discipline, pay), anything where a mistake cannot be undone, and anything that needs private data put into a public tool. A simple test for your team: would you be comfortable explaining to the person affected that AI did this?
Words to know:
- Hallucination: when AI writes something that sounds true but is made up.
- Bias: unfair patterns in AI output, often learned from its training data.
Try it now: List ten tasks your team does. Mark each GOOD, CARE or POOR for AI, with a few words on why.
You can now judge which of your team's tasks are good, careful or poor uses of AI.

options: A picture made by AI
AI refusing to answer
AI writing something that sounds true but is made up
AI running slowly
check.why: Hallucinations sound confident, which is why AI output needs checking.

check.q: Your team wants AI to decide which applicants get interviews. How would you mark it?
options: CARE or POOR: a person must make the decision, using AI only to help
GOOD: AI is faster
GOOD, as long as no one is told
Not worth thinking about
check.why: Decisions about people need human judgment, and the explain-it test fails if you would hide it.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Leading your team's first steps

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Risks every leader should name
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the main AI risks for your team and one guard for each.
This lesson builds toward: For your team's real work, you will name the three biggest AI risks and one guard for each, with guards you could put in place this month.
Privacy: anything typed into a public AI tool may be stored by the provider, and some free tools may use it to improve their products. Guard: no customer, employee or confidential data in public tools; use tools your organization has approved.
Accuracy: made-up facts, wrong numbers, invented sources. Guard: a person checks facts, figures and quotes before anything goes out. Bias and fairness: output can be unfair to groups of people. Guard: no AI-only decisions about people.
Security and agents: agents that read email or web pages can be tricked by hidden instructions (prompt injection), and agents with too much access can do real damage. Guard: least access and human approval for actions. For a fuller framework, NIST's free AI Risk Management Framework organizes this work into four functions: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage.
Words to know:
- Prompt injection: hidden text that tries to make an AI follow someone else's instructions.
- Least access: giving a tool or person only the access the job needs.
- NIST AI RMF: a free, voluntary US framework for managing AI risks.
Official sources:
- NIST AI Risk Management Framework
- OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025
Try it now: Write the three biggest AI risks for your team's actual work, and one guard you could put in place this month for each.
You can now name your team's main AI risks and a practical guard for each.

check.q: What does least access mean for AI tools?
options: Giving AI tools as much access as possible so they work well
Giving each tool only the access its job needs
Letting only the leader use AI
Using AI as little as possible
check.why: Least access limits the damage if a tool makes a mistake or is tricked.

check.q: Your team handles customer records. Which risk and guard pair fits best?
options: Risk: AI is slow. Guard: buy a faster computer
Risk: AI is new. Guard: wait five years
Risk: staff like AI. Guard: block all websites
Risk: personal details leak into public tools. Guard: remove details first or use an approved tool
check.why: A good guard matches the real risk in the team's own work.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Trying it yourself: a live demo you can show
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Run a short, safe AI demo on a real (non-private) team task.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free AI assistant and a non-private team task, you will run a short live demo, including one follow-up and a check, with no private data used.
Leaders who use AI themselves lead it better. Choose a real task with no private data: an agenda for next week's team meeting, a first draft of a job post, or a plain-language summary of a public policy.
Write a clear prompt: what you need, the context (no names or private details), and the format. Then improve it with one follow-up, such as "make it shorter" or "write it for new staff". Check every fact before you use it.
In your briefing, show the whole process, including a mistake if it makes one. Seeing a leader catch an AI error teaches the team more than a perfect demo.
Step by step:
- Pick a real task with no private data.
- Write a prompt: need, context, format.
- Ask one follow-up to improve it.
- Check facts and fix errors.
- Note what you would show the team.
Words to know:
- Prompt: what you type or say to an AI tool to ask for something.
- Follow-up: a second request that improves the first answer.
Try it now: Use ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini or Claude to draft next week's team meeting agenda. Ask one follow-up, check it, and save the before and after versions for your briefing.
You can now run a short, safe, honest AI demo on a real team task.

check.q: What makes a good live AI demo for your team?
options: A real task with no private data
A task using a real customer's file
A made-up task with no link to your work
A demo that hides any mistakes
check.why: A real but non-private task shows the value without putting anyone's data at risk.

check.q: During your demo the AI drafts an agenda with a wrong meeting date. What do you do?
options: Skip that part quickly
Blame the tool and stop
Show how you caught it and ask a follow-up to fix it
Say it is always this wrong
check.why: Showing the catch teaches your team the checking habit.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Briefing your team and setting a first ground rule
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Give a ten-minute team briefing on AI that ends with one ground rule.
This lesson builds toward: With your team, you will give a ten-minute AI briefing that ends with one ground rule, covering three uses, three risks and the rule, sent in writing afterwards.
A good first briefing is short and practical. Structure: two minutes on what AI and agentic AI are; three minutes of live demo; two minutes on good uses for our team; two minutes on risks; one minute on the ground rule and where to ask questions.
Choose one ground rule that protects people and is easy to remember. The most useful first rule for most teams: "No customer, client, student, patient or employee personal details go into public AI tools." Add who to ask when unsure.
Invite questions and worries. Some people will be excited, some anxious about their jobs. Say plainly what you know, what you do not, and that people stay accountable for their work. Then follow up in writing with the rule.
Step by step:
- Two minutes: what AI and agentic AI are.
- Three minutes: live demo.
- Two minutes: good uses for our team.
- Two minutes: risks.
- One minute: the ground rule and who to ask; then send it in writing.
Words to know:
- Ground rule: a simple, shared rule everyone follows.
- Briefing: a short meeting to give a team the same information.
Try it now: Final task: prepare your ten-minute briefing with the five parts above, using your demo from Lesson 5 and your risks from Lesson 4. Give it to your team (or record it), end with one ground rule, and send the rule in writing afterwards.
You can now brief your team on AI clearly and set a first ground rule that protects people.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Plain explanation Uses jargon, or mixes up generative and agentic AI. Explains generative and agentic AI in plain words. Uses an example from the team's own work that everyone recognizes. Three good uses Fewer than three uses, or uses that are poor fits. Names three good uses for the team's real work. Says which ones need a person to check the output. Three risks Risks are general or missing. Names three risks that fit the team's real work. Gives a guard for each risk. Live example No example, or it uses private data. Shows one live example with a free AI assistant on a non-private task. Shows a follow-up and how the output was checked. Ground rule No ground rule, or one that is vague. Ends with one clear ground rule everyone will follow. Names who to ask and sends the rule in writing afterwards. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What should a first AI briefing end with?
options: A list of every AI tool on the market
One clear ground rule and who to ask
A promise that AI will not change anything
A test with grades
check.why: One clear rule and a contact person give the team a shared starting point.

check.q: A day after your briefing, what is the best next step?
options: Wait to see if anyone remembers the rule
Add five more rules
Ask the AI to remind everyone
Send the ground rule to the team in writing
check.why: A written rule is easy to find and refer back to.
